name: Love Jones
description: Love Jones is a 1997 American romantic drama written and directed by Theodore Witcher in his feature directorial debut, set in Chicago's Black jazz and poetry scenes. Larenz Tate stars as Darius Lovehall, a poet and writer, opposite Nia Long as Nina Mosley, a photographer; the cast also includes Isaiah Washington, Lisa Nicole Carson, and Bill Bellamy. The Academy Museum describes the film as opening with a sequence of black-and-white photographs of Chicago, with the city itself as an immersive setting for a story of young Black professional and bohemian life, using Hyde Park and Wicker Park locations. Witcher developed the story from Chicago's underground poetry scene, and the film follows the tentative, on-again, off-again romance between Darius and Nina as they test whether early attraction can become a sustained relationship. The film won the audience award at the Sundance Film Festival, drew modest initial box office, and built a lasting cult following; decades later it was issued in the Criterion Collection in a new 4K restoration with new interviews, confirming its standing as a landmark of 1990s Black romance on screen.

name: Love Can't Turn Around
description: Love Can't Turn Around is a 1986 Chicago house recording by Farley “Jackmaster” Funk with producer Jesse Saunders, featuring the lead vocal of Darryl Pandy, released on Chicago's D.J. International Records. Farley built the track after hearing Steve “Silk” Hurley's house version of Isaac Hayes's “I Can't Turn Around”: he kept the bassline riff from Hayes's original, changed the hook from “I Can't Turn Around” to “Love Can't Turn Around,” and substituted new words by Vince Lawrence; through a later agreement with Universal Music, Hayes's song is now officially credited as the work's inspiration. Pandy, a Chicago singer with a Broadway and opera background, performed the song in its video and on Britain's Top of the Pops. Released in the United Kingdom by London Records, the record entered the UK Singles Chart in August 1986 and peaked at No. 10, becoming the first house record to cross over from American clubs onto the UK Singles Chart, and a 1996 re-release reached No. 40. Its success carried the Chicago house sound to a mainstream British audience years before house music charted at home.

description: Lena Horne (Lena Mary Calhoun Horne, born June 30, 1917, Brooklyn; died May 9, 2010, New York City, aged 92) joined the Cotton Club chorus at sixteen in 1933 and became one of the defining singers and screen presences of the twentieth century. name: Liz Torres
description: Puerto Rico-born, Chicago-raised house vocalist (b. Ponce; moved to Chicago at 3). Raised in a strictly religious home; sang in church; discovered house music on a Chicago beach via producer Jesse Jones. Debut 12" single "Mind Games" (1986); vocalist with Master C&J (Carl Bias & Jesse Jones) on "Can’t Get Enough" and "What You Make Me Feel" (released by DJ International Records). Counted among house music’s first real vocal talents and the most influential artists of the mid/late-80s Chicago house scene; performed at The Warehouse, the Paradise Garage, the Sound Factory, and Ministry of Sound.

name: Lester Barclay
description: Chicago attorney practicing family law (Case Western Reserve University School of Law, 1985; admitted Illinois bar 1985; Super Lawyers 2023–2025, 2027) who is the Honorary Consul of Jamaica in Chicago (4655 S Dr. Martin Luther King Drive, Suite 201), serving 60,000+ Jamaican nationals and residents. Honored by the Jamaican Consulate for community service in law; appointed to the Chicago Transit Board (term September 1, 2026–September 1, 2029); worked with State Rep. La Shawn Ford on Hurricane Melissa relief.

name: Loleatta Holloway
description: Chicago-born soul and disco singer (November 5, 1946 – March 21, 2011); began in gospel with Albertina Walker and the Caravans. Disco productions from 1976, mainly on Salsoul Records: "Love Sensation" (1980) re-launched her as a disco diva; sang on Dan Hartman’s "Relight My Fire"; four Club Play number ones. Black Box sampled "Love Sensation" on the UK number-one "Ride On Time" without credit — she sued and won a share of the royalties; properly credited on Marky Mark & the Funky Bunch’s "Good Vibrations" (1991). Left Salsoul in 1984; "Crash Goes Love" never completed.

name: Lil Hardin Armstrong
aliases: Hot Miss Lil; Lil Hardin; Lillian Beatrice Hardin; Lillian Hardin
description: Jazz pianist, composer, bandleader, and arranger (b. Lillian Beatrice Hardin, Memphis, February 3, 1898; d. Chicago, August 27, 1971). Pianist and arranger of King Oliver’s Creole Jazz Band in Chicago (1921–24); married fellow band member Louis Armstrong (February 5, 1924; divorced 1938), taught him to read music, and urged him to go solo; pianist and recording artist on Armstrong’s Hot Five sessions (1925–28); composed "Struttin’ with Some Barbeque." Led her own bands (Lil’s Dreamland Syncopators, Lil’s Hot Shots, the New Orleans Wanderers, Lil Hardin Armstrong and her Swing Orchestra); house pianist and recording artist for Decca Records (1931–40); died during a "St. Louis Blues" performance at a Louis Armstrong memorial concert in Chicago.

Co-founded the Five Breezes (1939), the Four Jumps of Jive, and the Big Three Trio (Columbia/Okeh) with Willie Dixon; best noted for "Blues at Midnight" and "I’m Gonna Walk Your Log." Reunited with Dixon in 1984; released Baby Doo’s House Party shortly before his death from heart disease in Minneapolis in 1987. Distinct from his son, guitarist Leonard Caston Jr.

Reinvented in 1918 by Black entrepreneurs Virgil Williams and William Bottoms; renamed Lincoln Gardens in 1921. Resident home of King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band (1922–1924), where Louis Armstrong came north to play second cornet. Closed June 1927 after a bombing.

name: Lake Ivanhoe, Wisconsin — Black-founded Chicago vacation community

CTL's everyday-life research records it as Wisconsin's first Black-founded resort community, a claim resting on a single secondary source. Its documented activity was vacationing and cottage ownership, and its generation was Black Chicago families of the 1920s through the 1960s. In the research package it stands as the nearby, less-expensive alternative to Idlewild, Michigan, for Black Chicago families, and its graph era runs from 1926 to 1969.

Exemplar: WVON’s ‘Good Guys’ era, from the station’s April 1, 1963 launch (canonical record CTL-E-0179): for more than a decade the Good Guys’ broadcasts made the station a daily presence and a voice of the civil rights movement in Black Chicago homes.

name: Listening to house-music radio mix shows

The mix shows started on WGCI and took off when WBMX answered with the Hot Mix 5 (1981); the Saturday-night five-hour shows drew up to a fifth of the city, and cassette recordings of the mixes spread worldwide.

Moved to Arkansas: Republican convention delegate (1870), Arkansas bar (1871), Pulaski County attorney, partner of Mifflin Gibbs. Influential in establishing Provident Hospital of Cook County. description: Lake Charles is a city in Calcasieu Parish, Louisiana, recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Locality with a Verified status. Its only documented connection in the record is contested. The graph describes it as the home of the Richard Funeral Home records held by the Center for Southeast Louisiana Studies, citing that Center as its primary source. The detailed preservation corpus, however, places Richard Funeral Home — a Black-owned funeral home whose funeral-program collection was donated to the Center in an arrangement made by Dr. Antoinette Harrell — in Amite, Louisiana, not Lake Charles, and the Center's own graph record places it at Southeastern Louisiana University in Hammond. name: Linn LM-1
description: The Linn LM-1 is a drum machine manufactured by Linn Electronics and released in 1980. It was the first programmable drum machine to use samples of acoustic drums, and only about 500 units were made; the graph record dates its production era to 1980–1983. CultureTechLens's technology research documents its designer, Roger Linn, as an inventor in his own right — CTL-DR-TECH-001 keeps Linn in the record precisely so the drum-machine transformation story is not misread as a Black invention, distinguishing the invention itself from the Black musical innovation that followed.

name: LinnDrum
description: The LinnDrum is a drum machine by Linn Electronics, released in 1982 as the successor to the LM-1. It was designed by Roger Linn, whom CultureTechLens's technology research credits with designing the LM-1, the LinnDrum, and — with Akai — the MPC60. CTL-DR-TECH-001 keeps Linn in the record for a distinction the project treats as load-bearing: he is the inventor of the tools, not of their hip-hop transformation — the transformation belongs to the Black musicians and producers who remade what the machines were for. Beyond that framing and the machine's place in the Linn line, CTL's corpus documents little about the LinnDrum itself: no specification sheet, production figures, or named-user accounts appear in the research files.

name: La Promesa Foundation
description: La Promesa Foundation is a Midland, Texas-based Catholic foundation, the operator of the Guadalupe Radio Network. In November 2012 it acquired Houston's KCOH (AM 1430) for $2.141 million — the purchase was consummated on February 28, 2013 — and launched Guadalupe Radio Network programming on the signal, ending the station's 59 years as a Black-owned outlet. KCOH had been, since Robert C. Meeker bought it in 1953, the first Black-owned radio station in Texas, reportedly the third in the nation, with all-Black programming. CultureTechLens's media research carries the foundation as the buyer in one of the defining losses of Black broadcast ownership.

name: Louis Carr
description: Louis Carr (born May 3, 1956, in Chicago, Illinois) is the president of BET — a Chicagoan running the flagship institution of Black television. A Lane Technical High School graduate (1974) who attended Drake University on a track scholarship and took a broadcast journalism degree in 1978, Carr worked at Johnson Publishing's Ebony from 1984 and at Black Enterprise in 1985 before being recruited to BET in 1986 as the company's thirty-third employee. Over thirty-nine years he rose through its advertising ranks — executive vice president of broadcast media sales, then the longtime president of media sales — building partnerships with the largest advertisers in America and generating advertising revenue reported in the billions across his tenure. On December 3, 2025, founder Robert L. Johnson announced Carr as President of BET, succeeding Scott Mills while continuing over media sales. Beyond the network, Carr founded the WayMaker initiative — its Men's Summit descends from his 2017 Dirty Little Secrets conference through the 2019 Blueprint summit — wrote Dirty Little Secrets and Little Black Book, and founded the Louis Carr Internship Foundation (2003), which has placed more than seventy students in media jobs.

name: L'Oreal
description: L'Oreal is a cosmetics conglomerate recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Business (manufacturing), Verified, with an era of 1998–present, under project RELP-001. Its documented place in the record is one acquisition: in 1998 the Gardner family sold SoftSheen-Carson to L'Oréal of Paris. SoftSheen-Carson had been formed in 1988 by merging Soft Sheen Products — Edward and Bettiann Gardner's Chicago Black hair-care company (founded 1964; Care Free Curl, Optimum) — with Carson Products. The graph record's shorter phrasing — L'Oreal 'acquired Soft Sheen Products in 1998, keeping the SoftSheen name while gaining access to the Black hair-care market' — compresses that sequence; the package's Verified claim (Black Enterprise; The HistoryMakers) gives the merged company as what was sold. The deal price is not verified in the corpus.

name: Lionel Hampton
description: Lionel Hampton was a bandleader who received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1988. His orchestra was a proving ground: Dinah Washington joined Hampton's band after winning a talent contest at Chicago's Regal Theater and playing the Garrick Stage Bar, and made her recording debut for Keynote Records in late 1943; tenor saxophonist Johnny Griffin also played with Hampton. Hampton himself appears on the Regal Theater's documented roster of notable performers of the 1920s–40s, alongside Louis Armstrong, Ella Fitzgerald, and Duke Ellington. By family account, the five-year-old Roy Ayers received his first vibraphone mallets from Hampton at a concert, an early link in the vibraphone lineage Ayers carried forward.

name: Leak & Sons
aliases: Leak & Sons Funeral Homes; Leak and Sons Funeral Homes; A.R. Leak Funeral Homes
description: Leak & Sons is a Black-owned, family-run funeral home business on Chicago's South Side, founded in 1933 by the Reverend A.R. Leak and his wife. The family's own history records that Leak first opened Unity Funeral Home in 1933, then established his own home at 44th and State Street; in 1959 the firm relocated to 78th and Cottage Grove, where its Chicago location stands today at 7838 S. Cottage Grove Avenue. Its founding promise — that every family, regardless of means, deserves to bury its loved ones with dignity — answered an era when Black Chicago families faced limited and unequal access to funeral services. Family and industry accounts also credit Rev. Leak with providing limousine service to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. during his Chicago campaigns and with helping lead the protest that desegregated Oak Woods Cemetery. After A.R. Leak's death in 1993, leadership passed to Spencer Leak Sr. and then to a third generation; the firm now operates three Illinois locations, in Chicago, Country Club Hills, and Matteson.

name: Larry Levan
description: Larry Levan (1954-1992) was a New York DJ and producer who learned the craft alongside Frankie Knuckles at the Continental Baths and became resident DJ at Paradise Garage, the defining Black and Latino gay dance club of its era. His long, dramatic, sound-system-centered sets are the closest comparison case for Knuckles's Warehouse practice. In the Warehouse story he appears as Robert Williams's reported first choice for the Chicago residency, an invitation Levan is said to have declined in favor of the Garage opening, and as the other half of the apprenticeship that formed Knuckles's approach to reading and moving a dancefloor over an entire night.

name: Lisa Blunt Rochester
description: Lisa LaTrelle Blunt Rochester (born February 10, 1962, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania) is the United States senator from Delaware. She built her career in Delaware state government — deputy secretary of Health and Social Services and secretary of Labor — before winning the state's at-large seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in 2016, becoming the first woman and the first person of color Delaware had ever sent to Congress. She served four terms in the House, from January 3, 2017, to January 3, 2025. In November 2024 she won the Senate seat left open by Tom Carper's retirement, and on January 3, 2025, she was sworn in as the first woman and the first Black person to represent Delaware in the United States Senate. Her election, with Angela Alsobrooks's in neighboring Maryland the same night, raised the number of Black senators serving simultaneously to five — the most in American history, and the spine of this record set. With Scott, Booker, Warnock, and Alsobrooks, she completes the five.

name: Loving v. Virginia decided (1967)
description: On June 12, 1967, the United States Supreme Court decided Loving v. Virginia, 388 U.S. 1, unanimously striking down Virginia's Racial Integrity Act and, with it, every remaining state law banning interracial marriage. Richard Loving, who was white, and Mildred Jeter Loving, who was Black and Native American, had married in Washington, D.C., in 1958 and returned home to Caroline County, Virginia, where they were indicted, pleaded guilty in January 1959 to violating the state's ban, and were sentenced to a year in prison — suspended for twenty-five years on condition they leave Virginia. They lived in exile in Washington and, with ACLU lawyers, carried the case from a Virginia courtroom to the Supreme Court, which held that marriage is a fundamental freedom and that racial restrictions on it serve no purpose other than invidious discrimination. Sixteen states still banned interracial marriage when the case was decided. This record carries the audit's correction on its face: the intake paste dated the ruling 1958 — the year of the marriage and the indictment — and the correct year, 1967, is what the graph now holds.

name: Los Angeles Riots (1992)
aliases: 1992 Los Angeles Riots; LA Riots; Los Angeles Uprising of 1992
description: On April 29, 1992, a California jury acquitted four Los Angeles police officers in the videotaped beating of Rodney King — a Black motorist whose March 3, 1991, beating by baton, boot, and Taser had been recorded by a bystander and broadcast around the world as early proof of what cameras would do to police violence. Within hours of the verdicts, Los Angeles erupted. Six days of rioting, looting, and arson spread across South Los Angeles and beyond; the California National Guard, federal troops, and Marines were deployed; more than sixty people died, thousands were injured, and property damage was estimated at roughly one billion dollars — the most destructive civil unrest in modern American history to that date. The uprising exposed the city's layered fractures — Black, Korean, and Latino communities ground against policing and disinvestment — and it stands in this timeline as the bridge between the movement era and the era of the bystander video, which the graph's later stops (CTL-E-5439) inherit. Rodney King himself holds no record in the graph; he is named here as the event's center, and stands as a future Person candidate.

name: Luke Cage (TV series)
description: Luke Cage, created and run by Cheo Hodari Coker and produced by Marvel Television with ABC Studios, premiered on Netflix on September 30, 2016, and released its second and final season on June 22, 2018 — two seasons, twenty-six episodes, the third of Marvel's Netflix series and the street-level Defenders strand's Black-led entry, set in Harlem rather than Hell's Kitchen, with Mike Colter's Cage having debuted in Jessica Jones. Its music was structural: a score and themes by Adrian Younge and Ali Shaheed Muhammad, episodes built around live musical performance, Harlem's club life functioning as the show's conscience. The series' afterlife is a documented case of streaming-era impermanence — on March 1, 2022, all of the Marvel Netflix series, this one included, left Netflix when the license lapsed, vanishing from the platform that had commissioned them. The graph files Luke Cage as the superhero shelf's Harlem entry: a bulletproof Black hero whose stories were about a neighborhood's rent, policing, and memory, and whose distribution fate is now part of television history itself.

name: Lu's Notebook
description: Lu's Notebook was the daily radio commentary program of Chicago journalist and activist Lu Palmer, heard on WVON and carried, according to his obituaries, on several stations. Palmer — a veteran of the Chicago Defender, the Chicago Daily News, and his own Black X-Press — developed the 'hard-hitting editorial newscast' after his newspaper years; its commentaries were heard, in the words of a Congressional Record memorial tribute, 'each and every day,' and when sponsors withdrew over their content, Palmer refused to be silenced. The Notebook often closed with his signature line, 'That's enough to make a Negro turn Black.' Paired with Palmer's late-evening WVON program On Target, it made him a drumbeat of Black Chicago's political awakening — the voice that coined 'We Shall See in '83,' the slogan of the movement that elected Harold Washington. Palmer retired from On Target in 2001.

name: Living Word Christian Center
aliases: LWCC; Living Word Church of Chicago
description: Living Word Christian Center is a nondenominational Word of Faith congregation in Forest Park, Illinois, founded by Dr. Bill Winston and his wife, Dr. Veronica Winston. The ministry began in 1988 with weekend Faith Crusades run from Minneapolis; the Winstons moved to Chicago that December and opened a Bible training school at the Quality Inn at Madison and Halsted, becoming the Living Word Church of Chicago in 1989 and Living Word Christian Center in 1990. After meeting at Forest Park's Chez Roué Banquet Hall from 1994 to 1997, the church bought the declining 33-acre Forest Park Mall and held its first service there on New Year's Eve 1997. Its worship center at 7600 West Roosevelt Road, built from the mall and its movie complex, anchors a campus that includes the Joseph Business School and the redeveloped Forest Park Plaza.

name: Latto
aliases: Alyssa Michelle Stephens; Miss Mulatto; Mulatto
description: Latto, born Alyssa Michelle Stephens on December 22, 1998, in Columbus, Ohio, and raised in Clayton County, Georgia, is a rapper who first won national attention at sixteen by winning the first season of the Lifetime reality competition The Rap Game in 2016, performing as Miss Mulatto. After independent releases, 'Bitch from da Souf' (2019) became her breakout single, later certified double platinum, and she signed with RCA Records ahead of her debut album Queen of Da Souf (2020). 'Big Energy' (2021) reached number three on the Billboard Hot 100 and was certified triple platinum; her second album 777 (2022) debuted at number fifteen on the Billboard 200, and she was nominated for Best New Artist at the 65th Grammy Awards. Her later run includes a featured turn on Jung Kook's Hot 100 number one 'Seven' (2023) and the album Sugar Honey Iced Tea (2024). CultureTechLens's Short covers 'Big Mama,' her 2024 single; the artist had no CultureTechLens record until this packet.

name: Lakesia Collins
description: Lakesia Collins (born 1985 in Chicago, Illinois) is an American union organizer and Democratic politician serving as Illinois state senator for the 5th district, on Chicago's West Side. A graduate of Proviso East High School in Maywood, she earned a Certified Nursing Assistant certificate from the Samland Institute in Chicago and worked in nursing homes before becoming an organizer with SEIU Healthcare Illinois, advocating nursing-home reform, a higher minimum wage, and the proposed Illinois Fair Tax. As a former youth in care who experienced housing insecurity, she has made youth in care and working families her legislative center. Collins won the March 2020 Democratic primary for the Illinois House's 9th district and was appointed to the seat that July — the first woman to represent the district. Appointed to the Senate on August 16, 2023, succeeding Patricia Van Pelt, she has since passed the Birth Equity Initiative (2024) and championed the KIND Act, signed in February 2025.

name: Larenz Tate
description: Larenz Tate (born September 8, 1975, on the West Side of Chicago, Illinois) is an American film and television actor, the youngest of three actor brothers — Larron and LahMard Tate (CTL-E-5582) are the others. His parents, Peggy and Larry Tate, moved the family to California in the early 1980s and enrolled the boys in a drama program at the Inner City Cultural Center; Tate made his television debut in 1985 in The Twilight Zone and took recurring roles on Family Matters and The Royal Family. His breakthrough came as O-Dog in the Hughes brothers' Menace II Society (1993), followed by Dead Presidents (1995) and the Chicago-set romantic drama Love Jones (1997), in which he played the poet Darius Lovehall. He went on to play Frankie Lymon in Why Do Fools Fall in Love (1998) and Quincy Jones in Ray (2004), appear in Crash (2004), and reach a new audience as Councilman Rashad Tate on Power (2017–2020) and Power Book II: Ghost (2020–2024).

name: LahMard Tate
description: LahMard Tate (also credited as Lahmard J. Tate) is an American actor and the older brother of actor Larenz Tate (CTL-E-5581); with their brother Larron, the Tate brothers were raised in Chicago and, after the family moved to California, trained at the Inner City Cultural Center. His screen career runs from the late 1980s — early credits include Barfly (1987) and Hill Street Blues — through a steady run of 1990s work: Across the Tracks, Jason's Lyric (1994), Panther (1995), and a turn as Ashtray's father in Don't Be a Menace to South Central While Drinking Your Juice in the Hood (1996). He is best known to wider audiences as Billy, the accomplice in the stolen-ATM subplot of Barbershop (2002); he later played Leon in the television film Sabretooth and appeared in Rocky Balboa (2006) and The Janky Promoters (2009). This record is staged Provisional: his filmography is documented by film references, but no authoritative biographical source fixes his vital details, and published birth dates conflict (see notes).

name: Laura Jarrett
description: Laura Jarrett is an American journalist and attorney, the daughter of Valerie Jarrett, the longtime adviser to President Barack Obama, and a co-anchor of NBC's Saturday TODAY. Raised in Chicago, she graduated from Amherst College and earned her law degree from Harvard Law School. She began her career in Chicago as a litigator at a national law firm, where her practice included defending clients facing Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission investigations, and she built a substantial pro bono practice representing people seeking expungement of criminal records. She joined CNN in 2016 as a justice correspondent, covering the Justice Department, the courts, and the Russia investigation, and developed a reputation for careful, source-driven legal reporting. In January 2023 she moved to NBC News as a senior legal correspondent covering the Supreme Court and the Justice Department. Later in 2023 she was named co-anchor of Saturday TODAY alongside Peter Alexander. She has also served as a legal analyst across NBC platforms. Her reporting treats the law as a civic subject, translating litigation and institutional process for a general audience.

name: LaRoyce Hawkins
description: LaRoyce Hawkins (born May 4, 1988) is an American actor, stand-up comic, spoken-word artist, and musician from Harvey, Illinois, a south suburb of Chicago. Raised by his grandparents until age 13, he played basketball and studied theatre at Thornton High School, winning state titles in speech original comedy with the Thornton Speech Team, then attended Illinois State University on a full-tuition artistic scholarship, majoring in acting. He made his film debut as Art Baker in The Express: The Ernie Davis Story (2008) while still a student. After early roles including HBO's Ballers, he was cast in 2014 as Officer Kevin Atwater on NBC's Chicago P.D., the role that made him a fixture of Chicago television; he played Atwater for more than a decade, a tenure that ended with his departure from the series in October 2026, when his final episode aired in season fourteen. He has mentored Chicago youth through his #BePowerful initiative and recorded spoken-word and music alongside his screen career, and he served as a Made in Chicago speaker for the Goodman Theatre.

name: Lil Rel Howery
description: Lil Rel Howery, born Milton Howery Jr. on December 17, 1979, is an American comedian and actor from the West Side of Chicago. He attended Providence St. Mel School and Crane High School, where a senior-year talent show script turned him toward comedy professionally; his nickname came from his resemblance to an older cousin, Darrel. Howery began performing stand-up in Chicago clubs and made his television debut on Last Comic Standing in 2007. He co-starred as Bobby Carmichael on NBC's The Carmichael Show (2015–2017), then broke out as TSA officer Rod Williams in Jordan Peele's Get Out (2017), winning the MTV Movie & TV Award for Best Comedic Performance. He created and starred in the Fox sitcom Rel (2018–2019), played Buddy in Free Guy (2021), and released the stand-up specials RELevent (Netflix, 2016), Live in Crenshaw (HBO, 2019), and I Said It. Y'all Thinking It (HBO, 2022), the last filmed in Chicago.

name: Laila Ali
aliases: Laila Amaria Ali; She Bee Stingin'
description: Laila Ali, born Laila Amaria Ali on December 30, 1977, in Miami Beach, Florida, is an American retired professional boxer and television personality, the daughter of Muhammad Ali and Veronica Porché Ali. She earned a business degree from Santa Monica College and owned a nail salon before turning to boxing, against her father's initial wishes. Ali made her professional debut in October 1999 with a first-round knockout and built the defining women's boxing career of her era: in June 2001 she defeated Jacqui Frazier-Lyde, Joe Frazier's daughter, in the first pay-per-view event headlined by women; she won the IBA super middleweight title in 2002, added the WIBA and IWBF super middleweight titles, the IWBF light heavyweight title in 2004, and the WBC super middleweight title in 2005. She retired in 2007 undefeated at 24 wins, no losses, with 21 knockouts, and was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2021. Her second career in television includes hosting and competing across lifestyle, cooking, and sports programming.

name: Lil' Kim
aliases: Kimberly Denise Jones; Kimberly Jones; Queen Bee
description: Lil' Kim (born Kimberly Denise Jones on July 11 in Brooklyn, New York — her birth year is carried as 1974, with 1975 in some listings) is the rapper whose explicit, fashion-forward persona reset what a woman MC could say and sell. Discovered by The Notorious B.I.G. in 1994, she debuted with his group Junior M.A.F.I.A. on Conspiracy (1995). Her solo debut Hard Core (1996) was certified double platinum and produced three consecutive number-one rap hits — "No Time," "Not Tonight (Ladies Night Remix)" and "Crush on You" — a record for a female rapper. The "Not Tonight" remix put her on record with Da Brat, Missy Elliott, Angie Martinez and Lisa "Left Eye" Lopes. In 2001 "Lady Marmalade" topped the Billboard Hot 100, making her the first female rapper to reach number one on that chart, and won the Grammy for Best Pop Collaboration with Vocals. name: Lil Wayne

description: Lil Wayne (born Dwayne Michael Carter Jr. on September 27, 1982, in New Orleans, Louisiana) is the defining rapper of his generation — signed at twelve, a platinum soloist at seventeen, and the genre's center of gravity by 2008. Birdman signed him to Cash Money Records in 1995, making him the label's youngest member; he joined the Hot Boys in 1997 and broke solo with Tha Block Is Hot (1999). After Tha Carter (2004) and Tha Carter II (2005) and a relentless mixtape run, Tha Carter III (2008) sold more than a million copies in its first week, topped the Billboard 200 and won the Grammy for Best Rap Album, carried by "Lollipop" and "A Milli." Through his Young Money imprint he launched Drake and Nicki Minaj, and in August 2012 he passed Elvis Presley as the male artist with the most Billboard Hot 100 entries. name: Leon Cox
description: Leon Cox is a name carried at position 19 of the Fill 500 “Comedians” bucket in the 747 Supply Ledger — the mixed Chicago civic list whose identified entries run from aldermen and athletes to broadcasters and artists. This record is staged PROVISIONAL because the identification is UNRESOLVED: three research passes for this packet (Chicago gospel and WVON broadcasting; comedians and obituary records; Chicago journalism) returned only namesakes — among them a Texas gospel broadcaster and several unrelated obituaries — and none could be documented as the person the founder's list intends. No biographical claim is asserted for Leon Cox anywhere in this record, and no relationship is staged. The name is held in the graph exactly as the ledger carries it, so the list's completeness is preserved without inventing a biography. Resolution requires the list's original source or an archival check (Chicago Defender or WVON records) that ties this name to a documented Chicago figure; on that evidence the record can be completed or corrected at enrichment.

name: La Toya Jackson
aliases: La Toya Yvonne Jackson; LaToya Jackson
description: La Toya Jackson, born La Toya Yvonne Jackson on 29 May 1956 at St Mary's Mercy Hospital in Gary, Indiana, is an American singer and television personality, the fifth of the ten Jackson children. She first appeared on the family's CBS variety show The Jacksons (1976–77) and became the first female Jackson sibling to pursue a solo recording career, debuting with La Toya Jackson (1980) on Polydor. Her breakthrough album Heart Don't Lie (1984) produced her highest-charting US single, the title duet with Howard Hewett, which peaked at No. 56 on the Hot 100. She sang on USA for Africa's "We Are the World" (1985) and released nine studio albums over fifteen years. Her later career spans a bestselling 1991 autobiography, the OWN series Life with La Toya (2013–14), and reality formats including Celebrity Apprentice and The Masked Singer.

aliases: Lionel Brockman Richie Jr.; Lionel Richie Jr.
description: Lionel Richie, born Lionel Brockman Richie Jr. on 20 June 1949 in Tuskegee, Alabama, is an American singer and songwriter. A founding member of the Commodores at Motown — saxophonist, vocalist and writer of "Easy," "Three Times a Lady" and "Still" — he went solo with Lionel Richie (1982), whose "Truly" won his first Grammy. Can't Slow Down (1983) won the Grammy for Album of the Year; he co-wrote "We Are the World" (1985) with Michael Jackson and won the Academy Award for "Say You, Say Me." Tuskegee (2012) returned him to No. 1 on the Billboard 200, he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, and his memoir Truly was published on 30 September 2025 alongside a continuing American Idol judgeship and a 2026 North American tour.

name: Lil Uzi Vert
description: Lil Uzi Vert, born Symere Bysil Woods on 31 July in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, is an American rapper whose birth year is given as "1994 or 1995" in the reference record itself and is carried here as disputed. The mixtape Luv Is Rage (2015) led to Atlantic Records through DJ Drama's Generation Now, with later Roc Nation management. "Money Longer" (2016) broke them nationally; a feature on Migos' No. 1 "Bad and Boujee" and the solo top-ten hit "XO Tour Llif3" (2017) followed. Three consecutive solo albums topped the Billboard 200 — Luv Is Rage 2 (2017), Eternal Atake (2020) and Pink Tape (2023), the last opening with 167,000 units as the first rap No. 1 of 2023. They were Grammy-nominated for Best New Artist in 2018, and Eternal Atake 2 (2024) debuted at No. 3.

description: Lil Baby, born Dominique Armani Jones on 3 December 1994 in Atlanta, Georgia, is an American rapper. He rose through 2017 mixtapes — Perfect Timing, Harder Than Hard, Too Hard — signed to Quality Control Music under Motown and Capitol, and founded his own 4PF imprint. His debut Harder Than Ever (2018) carried the Drake-featuring "Yes Indeed"; the Gunna joint mixtape Drip Harder (2018) and The Voice of the Heroes with Lil Durk (2021) followed. My Turn (2020) spent five weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and was the best-selling album of 2020 in secondary counts; "The Bigger Picture" (2020) reached No. 3 on the Hot 100. WHAM, released 3 January 2025, debuted at No. 1 with 140,000 units — his fourth No. 1 album — and he won the Grammy for Best Melodic Rap Performance for Kanye West's "Hurricane" in 2022.

aliases: Alani Nicole Vázquez; Alani Vázquez; La La
description: La La Anthony, born Alani Nicole Vázquez in Brooklyn, New York City, is an American television personality and actress of Puerto Rican parentage who describes herself as Afro-Puerto Rican. She began in Atlanta radio as a teenager, co-hosting alongside Ludacris, before becoming an MTV VJ in the early 2000s, notably on Total Request Live. She hosted VH1 reunion franchises including Flavor of Love and I Love New York and starred in her own VH1 series La La's Full Court Life. As an actress she played Lakeisha Grant, a series-regular role from season three of Starz's Power, and plays Markisha Taylor in Starz's BMF, covered in its fourth season by Essence in June 2025. Her birth date is carried as 25 June with the year unresolved: sources give 1979 and 1982 in parallel, and one listing gives a conflicting day — the conflict is documented in this record rather than blended into a single asserted date.

name: Life Center COGIC
aliases: Life Center Church of God in Christ; The Life Center C.O.G.I.C.; Life Center Church of Universal Awareness; The Prayer Palace
description: Life Center COGIC — the Life Center Church of God in Christ, known to its congregation as the Prayer Palace — is a Pentecostal congregation at 5500 South Indiana Avenue in Chicago's Washington Park neighborhood, led for nearly five decades by Pastor T. L. Barrett. Barrett began pastoring in 1966 and led Mt. Zion Baptist Church, at 5512 South Indiana Avenue, from the late 1960s; after a theological disagreement with that church's elders, he left in 1976 to form his own ministry, the Life Center COGIC church, in the same neighborhood. The congregation is the institutional home of Barrett's youth-focused ministry, the work carried on the records of Pastor T.L. Barrett and the Youth for Christ Choir, whose 1970s gospel recordings later drew a national audience. Barrett's congregation remained with him through the court-ordered restitution of the 1990s, which he completed, and in April 2024 the church community marked his stepping back from the pulpit with a three-day celebration honoring Barrett and his wife, Cleopatra Barrett, including a gospel concert at Life Center COGIC.

name: Leah Jeffries
description: Leah Jeffries, born Leah Sava Jeffries on 25 September 2009 in Detroit, Michigan, is an American actress who began as a child model before making her acting debut as Lola on the musical drama Empire (2015). She made her feature-film debut in the thriller Beast (2022) and appeared the same year in Something from Tiffany's. In May 2022 Disney+ announced her casting as Annabeth Chase, the daughter of Athena, in Percy Jackson and the Olympians, its series adaptation of Rick Riordan's novels, alongside Walker Scobell as Percy and Aryan Simhadri as Grover. The role, which she has continued through the series' subsequent seasons, earned her NAACP Image Award recognition and a Children's and Family Emmy nomination for Outstanding Younger Performer, per her biographical record.

name: Lady Soul
description: Lady Soul is an Aretha Franklin album released on January 22, 1968, by Atlantic Records, produced by Jerry Wexler with Tom Dowd as recording engineer. Recorded with players including Eric Clapton, Bobby Womack, and Cissy Houston and the Sweet Inspirations, it was Franklin's follow-up to her two 1967 Atlantic hit albums and became her second R&B chart-topping album, peaking at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 — tied for her highest position on that chart — and at No. 1 on the soul albums chart. Its singles carried the record: 'Chain of Fools' reached No. 2 on the pop chart, '(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman' reached No. 8, and '(Sweet Sweet Baby) Since You've Been Gone' reached No. 5, alongside her readings of Curtis Mayfield's 'People Get Ready' and her sister Carolyn Franklin's 'Ain't No Way.' The album sold over a million copies in the United States and was ranked No. 75 on Rolling Stone's revised 2020 list of the 500 greatest albums.

name: Land of Hope
aliases: Land of Hope: Chicago, Black Southerners, and the Great Migration
description: Land of Hope: Chicago, Black Southerners, and the Great Migration is a history book by James R. Grossman, published by the University of Chicago Press — in cloth in 1989 and in the 398-page paperback edition dated February 1991 that this record's era follows. Drawing on government records, manuscripts, and other archival material, the book studies Black Southerners who migrated to Chicago during World War I and its aftermath, treating the movement as a cultural as well as economic experience: why migrants left, what they expected the North to be, and how they remade their lives, work, and institutions in the city. It is organized in two parts, the second describing how the Southerners lived once in Chicago, and it has been received in the scholarly community as a significant contribution to the history of Black migration to Chicago. Grossman later served as executive director of the American Historical Association and as a director of the Encyclopedia of Chicago project.

name: Love Is the Thing
description: Love Is the Thing is a 1957 studio album by American jazz vocalist Nat King Cole, released by Capitol Records in April 1957 and recorded on December 19 and 28, 1956, at Capitol's Hollywood studio. It was the first of four collaborations between Cole and arranger Gordon Jenkins, whose orchestra accompanies Cole throughout, and it was produced by Lee Gillette. The twelve-track original album presents Cole exclusively as a ballad singer, pairing his restrained vocal approach with Jenkins's unhurried string charts on standards including "When I Fall in Love," "Stardust," and the title track. "Stardust" was issued as the album's charting single. The record reached No. 1 on Billboard's Pop Albums chart and, according to RIAA records, achieved gold status in 1960 and platinum in 1992; it was Cole's first gold album. Cole and Jenkins went on to make three further albums together: The Very Thought of You (1958), Every Time I Feel the Spirit (1959), and Where Did Everyone Go? (1963). Discogs release records for the original Capitol pressing (catalogue W 824) confirm Jenkins's arranger-conductor credit and the twelve-song program of the 1957 mono LP.

name: Lonzo Ball
description: Lonzo Ball, born Lonzo Anderson Ball on 27 October 1997 in Anaheim, California, is an American point guard whose career has been shaped by elite playmaking and a persistent left-knee injury. At Chino Hills High School he played alongside his brothers LiAngelo and LaMelo on a team that finished 35-0 in his senior season and took consensus national honors. In one season at UCLA he led the nation in assists, set the school single-season assists record, earned consensus first-team All-American honors and won the Wayman Tisdale Award. The Los Angeles Lakers selected him second overall in the 2017 NBA draft, and he made the NBA All-Rookie Second Team in 2018. Traded to New Orleans in 2019 in the Anthony Davis deal, he played two seasons for the Pelicans before joining the Chicago Bulls in a 2021 sign-and-trade. A meniscus tear in January 2022 and a cartilage transplant in March 2023 cost him the full 2022-23 and 2023-24 seasons; he returned for 35 games with Chicago in 2024-25, then played 35 games for Cleveland in 2025-26 before a February 2026 trade and waiver left him a free agent.

name: Lamar Odom
description: Lamar Odom, born Lamar Joseph Odom on 6 November 1979 in Jamaica, Queens, New York, is an American former forward whose versatility made him a cornerstone of a championship team. Parade's national high school player of the year in 1997, he played one season at the University of Rhode Island before the Los Angeles Clippers selected him fourth overall in the 1999 NBA draft; he made the NBA All-Rookie First Team. After four seasons with the Clippers and one with the Miami Heat, he was traded to the Los Angeles Lakers in 2004 and spent seven seasons there, winning back-to-back championships in 2009 and 2010 and the NBA Sixth Man of the Year award in 2011. He later played for Dallas and again for the Clippers, and briefly in Spain in 2014, closing a 14-season career with averages of 13.3 points, 8.4 rebounds and 3.7 assists in 961 games. With the United States national team he won Olympic bronze in 2004 and FIBA World Championship gold in 2010. In October 2015 he was found unconscious in Nevada and hospitalized in a coma; he recovered and has spoken publicly since about addiction and recovery, most recently in a 2026 Netflix documentary.

name: Lamar Jackson
description: Lamar Jackson, born Lamar Demeatrice Jackson Jr. on 7 January 1997 in Pompano Beach, Florida, is an American football quarterback for the Baltimore Ravens and the defining dual-threat quarterback of his generation. At the University of Louisville he won the Heisman Trophy in 2016, becoming the youngest winner in the award's history at the time and the first Cardinal to claim it. Baltimore selected him with the final pick of the first round, 32nd overall, in the 2018 NFL Draft, and he became the starter during his rookie season. In 2019, his first full season as a starter, he led the NFL in touchdown passes, set the single-season rushing record for a quarterback, and was voted NFL Most Valuable Player unanimously. He won a second MVP award for the 2023 season, when he led Baltimore to the AFC Championship Game, and in 2024 he set career highs in passing and became the NFL's all-time leader in rushing yards by a quarterback. He remained Baltimore's starting quarterback in the 2026 season.

name: L. Alex Wilson
description: L. Alex Wilson (Lucious Alexander Wilson) was the editor and general manager of the Memphis Tri-State Defender and one of the Black press's defining correspondents of the civil rights era. He covered the Korean War for the Chicago Defender in 1950, led the Defender newspaper chain's coverage of the Emmett Till case in 1955, and hired Dorothy Butler Gilliam, who became a pioneering Black woman journalist. On September 23, 1957, covering the Little Rock Nine in Arkansas, Wilson was beaten by a white mob on camera — struck with a brick and choked — and refused to run, an image of press courage carried on national television. He later became editor of the Chicago Defender. The 1957 assault's injuries shadowed the rest of his life; he died in 1960 at 51, of Parkinson's disease that the sources tie to the beating's damage. His birth year is not independently sourced in the accounts read and is shown only as the arithmetic of his reported age at death.

name: Let's Get It On
description: Let's Get It On is the twelfth studio album by singer and songwriter Marvin Gaye, released August 28, 1973, on Tamla, the Motown subsidiary label. Recorded in Detroit at Hitsville U.S.A. and Golden World and in Los Angeles at Hitsville West across sessions running from 1970 into 1973, and produced by Gaye with Ed Townsend, the eight-track album followed the socially conscious What's Going On with a turn toward funk, smooth soul, and songs of desire that Gaye framed in spiritual terms. Its singles were the title track, a number-one pop and R&B hit, 'Come Get to This,' and 'You Sure Love to Ball.' The album became the most commercially successful of Gaye's Motown career, widened his creative control at the label, and helped establish the slow-jam idiom in later R&B. It was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2004 and reissued in expanded editions, including a 50th-anniversary release in 2023.

name: Larry Holmes
description: Larry Holmes, born 3 November 1949 in Cuthbert, Georgia, and raised in Easton, Pennsylvania, is an American former professional boxer known as the Easton Assassin. A former sparring partner for Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier, he turned professional in 1973 and won the WBC heavyweight title in June 1978 by outpointing Ken Norton over fifteen rounds in one of the division's greatest fights. Built around one of the finest left jabs in boxing history, his reign lasted more than seven years and included twenty successful title defenses, a total surpassed among heavyweights only by Joe Louis. His defense against Ali in 1980 made him the only boxer ever to stop Ali. He lost the title to Michael Spinks in 1985, one win short of Rocky Marciano's 49-0 mark, challenged for titles into his forties, and fought finally in 2002 with a record of 69 wins and 6 losses. He was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2008.

name: Laurie Hernandez
description: Laurie Hernandez, born 9 June 2000 in New Brunswick, New Jersey to Puerto Rican parents and raised in Old Bridge Township, is an American retired artistic gymnast. She won the U.S. junior all-around titles at the 2015 U.S. Classic and national championships, then at Rio 2016, at sixteen, helped the “Final Five” win the team gold medal and took an individual silver medal on balance beam. Later in 2016 she won Dancing with the Stars, the show's youngest champion. Hernandez identifies as Afro-Latina: in a published interview she described embracing her Afro-Boricua roots and said she identifies as Afro-Latina, a self-identification this record rests on for its scope basis. She attempted a comeback before retiring on 6 June 2021, then built a second career as an author of two New York Times best-sellers, an NBC gymnastics analyst at the Tokyo and Paris Olympics, a UNICEF USA Ambassador, and a stage performer — making her Broadway debut in & Juliet in spring 2026 and performing Off-Broadway in The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee in autumn 2026.

name: Lewis Hamilton
aliases: Lewis Carl Davidson Hamilton; Sir Lewis Hamilton
description: Sir Lewis Carl Davidson Hamilton, born 7 January 1985 in Stevenage, England, is a British Formula One driver for Ferrari and, with Michael Schumacher, the joint-most successful driver in the sport's history. The son of Anthony Hamilton, whose parents emigrated from Grenada to Britain in the 1950s, and Carmen Larbalestier, he was signed to McLaren's young driver programme in 1998 and reached Formula One in 2007 as the series' first Black driver. He missed the title by one point as a rookie, then won the 2008 championship, becoming the first Black driver to win it. After moving to Mercedes in 2013 he won six further titles — 2014, 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2020 — to tie Schumacher's record of seven. He holds the Formula One records for race wins, pole positions and podium finishes. Hamilton joined Ferrari in 2025; his first season there was his first without a Grand Prix podium, and he took his first Ferrari podium with third place at the 2026 Chinese Grand Prix. Through his Mission 44 foundation and his campaigning for a Grand Prix in Africa, he remains the sport's leading voice on diversity.

name: Louis Allen
description: Louis Allen, born 25 April 1919 in Amite County, Mississippi, was an African American logger and businessman in Liberty, Mississippi, and a World War II veteran. In September 1961 he witnessed the murder of his friend Herbert Lee, a farmer active with the NAACP and SNCC voter-registration work, who was shot at a Liberty cotton gin by Mississippi state representative E. H. Hurst. Pressured by local authorities, Allen gave testimony supporting Hurst's self-defense claim, and a coroner's jury cleared Hurst. Allen later told federal investigators and civil rights workers the truth and said he would testify if the government protected him; the Justice Department declined. Word of his cooperation spread, his logging business was boycotted, he received death threats, and Amite County Sheriff Daniel Jones harassed and jailed him repeatedly, once breaking his jaw. Allen stayed to care for his elderly mother, then planned to move to Milwaukee. On 31 January 1964, the night before he was to leave, he was shot and killed at the gate of his home. No one was ever prosecuted for his murder.

name: Loni Love
description: Loni Love, born 12 July 1971 in Detroit, Michigan, is an American comedian, television host, actress and author who came to comedy by an unusual road: electrical engineering. A graduate of Prairie View A&M University, she worked as an engineer for a decade while performing stand-up, finished as runner-up on Star Search in 2003, and was named one of the 'Top 10 Comics to Watch' by Comedy Central and Variety. From 2013 to 2022 she co-hosted the syndicated daytime talk show The Real, winning the 2018 Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Entertainment Talk Show Host, alongside two NAACP Image Awards and three Gracie Awards. She has written two books — Love Him or Leave Him but Don't Get Stuck with the Tab (2013) and the memoir I Tried to Change So You Don't Have To (2020) — and in 2019 became the first woman to host the mainstage of the Essence Festival. She remains an active touring stand-up in 2026.

name: LaVar Ball
description: LaVar Christopher Ball, born 23 October 1967 in Los Angeles, California, is an American businessman and media personality, the co-founder and chief executive of the sports apparel company Big Baller Brand and the founder of the Junior Basketball Association. A former college basketball player at West Los Angeles College, Washington State and Cal State Los Angeles, he also spent time on the practice squads of the New York Jets and Carolina Panthers and played for the London Monarchs, without appearing in an NFL regular-season game. He co-founded Big Baller Brand in 2016 as his sons Lonzo, LiAngelo and LaMelo rose through Chino Hills High School, launched the Junior Basketball Association in 2017 as an alternative route for high-school graduates, and fronted the family's Facebook Watch series Ball in the Family. In February 2025 he underwent amputation of his right foot and part of his lower right leg after a diabetes-related infection, describing three surgeries and four blood transfusions in a first-person account for SLAM. By the summer of 2026 he was again speaking publicly as the brand's head, saying in July 2026 that he had refused an offer to take Big Baller Brand public.

name: Liam Charles
description: Liam Charles, born 28 August 1997 in Hackney, London, is a British baker, television presenter and author of Caribbean background. A drama student at Goldsmiths, University of London, who began baking at sixteen and was nicknamed 'Cake Boy' at school, he came to national attention as a contestant on series eight of The Great British Bake Off in 2017, finishing fifth. Channel 4 built a presenting career on that run: he has co-presented Bake Off: The Professionals since 2018, fronted his own series Liam Bakes that year, and judged Junior Bake Off since 2019. His two cookbooks, Cheeky Treats (2018) and Second Helpings (2019), fold the food of his upbringing — his grandmother's curried goat, jerk chicken, ackee and salt fish — into contemporary baking, and he has spoken in interviews about baking while Black and about the shortage of high-profile Caribbean bakers, saying he hopes to change that. He also writes a baking column for The Guardian and appeared on The Masked Dancer in 2022; roundups of Bake Off's most successful contestants published in 2026 still list him in his Professionals and Junior Bake Off roles.

name: Lafayette Leake
description: Lafayette Leake (June 1, 1919 – August 14, 1990) was a Chicago blues and jazz pianist, organist, vocalist and composer. Born in Winona, Mississippi — some derivative sources give Missouri, and his birth year is sometimes given as about 1920 — he enters the documented record in the early 1950s, when he replaced Leonard "Baby Doo" Caston in Willie Dixon's Big Three Trio and began his association with Chess Records. As a Chess session musician from the 1950s through the 1970s, Leake played piano on Chuck Berry's One Dozen Berrys (1958) and on Berry Is on Top (1959), where his piano, not Johnnie Johnson's, carries the original recording of "Johnny B. Goode". He also backed Sonny Boy Williamson, Otis Rush, Junior Wells and Little Walter. In the 1960s Dixon made him resident pianist of the Chicago Blues All-Stars, with whom he toured and recorded until the mid-1970s. Leake appeared with Berry at the 1986 Chicago Blues Festival and recorded Dixon's Hidden Charms in 1988. He died in a Chicago hospital in 1990 after a diabetic coma at home.

name: Leland Giants
aliases: Chicago Leland Giants; Chicago Union Giants
description: The Leland Giants were a Chicago Negro league baseball team formed in 1901 by the merger of the Chicago Unions and the Chicago Columbia Giants, competing independently during the first decade of the twentieth century. First called the Chicago Union Giants, the team was renamed for owner-manager Frank Leland before the 1905 season. Catcher Bruce Petway joined in 1906, and talent rose sharply in 1907 as Rube Foster, Big Bill Gatewood and other players arrived from East Coast teams; Pete Hill was added in 1908, when the club went 64–21 against semipro teams. Foster managed the team in 1909, and that October the Lelands played the Chicago Cubs closely, losing two one-run decisions and another close game. In 1910 the club split: Foster retained the Leland Giants side — one source credits Foster, another credits Beauregard Moseley, with winning the rights to the name — while Leland's new team became the Chicago Giants. That 1910 club said it went 123–6 overall. In 1911 the club was renamed the Chicago American Giants and moved to Schorling's Park, the former South Side Park; before 1911 it had played mainly at the earlier Auburn Park grounds at 79th and Wentworth.

name: Lala Baptiste
description: Nyela Baptiste, born 16 May 1999 in Atlanta, Georgia, is an American model and social media influencer known as Lala Baptiste. Of African-American and Trinidadian descent, with Trinidadian roots through her mother Simone Baptiste, she posted her first Instagram photograph in April 2016 and built a following of more than one million on the platform as @lalatheislandgal, modelling for online fashion brands and working as a brand ambassador. She expanded into YouTube vlogging and, in December 2020, launched her own clothing label, the Nyela Collection, which she designed and funded herself. Her public profile grew through appearances in music videos and collaborations with recording artists. In 2025 she began a public relationship with rapper and streamer Jay Cinco; the couple announced they were expecting a child in December 2025, became engaged at their livestreamed baby shower in March 2026, welcomed a daughter, and announced an amicable separation in October 2026.

name: Leslie Jones
description: Annette Leslie Jones, born September 7, 1967, in Memphis, Tennessee, is an American stand-up comedian and actress. She began stand-up in college in 1987 after winning a 'Funniest Person on Campus' contest, performed at comedy clubs while working day jobs, and in 2010 broadcast her one-hour special Problem Child on Showtime. She was a cast member and writer for NBC's Saturday Night Live from 2014 to 2019, joining the cast at age 47 — the oldest person to join the show as a cast member at that time — after first being hired as a writer. She starred in Ghostbusters (2016) as Patty Tolan, and later appeared in Coming 2 America and Good Burger 2. In 2017 and 2018 she was nominated for the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series for her work on Saturday Night Live, and NBC Sports counts three Primetime Emmy nominations for her SNL work in total. In 2017 she hosted the BET Awards and was named to TIME magazine's list of the 100 most influential people. She has reprised her Olympics super-fan commentator role for NBC in 2016, 2018 and 2024.

name: Leon Sullivan
aliases: Leon Howard Sullivan Jr.; Leon H. Sullivan; Rev. Leon Sullivan; The Lion of Zion
description: The Reverend Leon Howard Sullivan Jr., born October 16, 1922, in Charleston, West Virginia, was a Baptist minister, civil-rights leader, and corporate reformer. A foot injury ended the athletic scholarships that took him to West Virginia State College. Ordained as a Baptist minister at eighteen, he studied at Union Theological Seminary and Columbia University, and in 1950 became pastor of Philadelphia's Zion Baptist Church, which he led until 1988 as its membership grew from 600 to over 6,000. In Philadelphia he led selective-patronage boycotts against employment discrimination and, in 1964, founded the Opportunities Industrialization Centers, a self-help job-training program begun in an abandoned Philadelphia jail. In 1971 he joined the board of General Motors, becoming the first African American on the board of a major corporation. From that position he authored the Sullivan Principles in 1977, a code of conduct for companies operating in apartheid South Africa, extended in 1999 as the Global Sullivan Principles issued at the United Nations. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1992. He died of leukemia on April 24, 2001, in Scottsdale, Arizona.

name: Louis B. Anderson
description: Louis Bernard Anderson, born April 17, 1870, in Petersburg, Virginia, was the Chicago lawyer, journalist, and Republican politician who represented the 2nd Ward — most of the Douglas community area, including much of Bronzeville — on the Chicago City Council from 1917 to 1933. He came to Chicago in 1892 as an assistant for the World's Columbian Exposition, graduated from Chicago-Kent College of Law in 1897, befriended Robert S. Abbott, and became a contributing editor of Abbott's Chicago Defender. Elected alderman in 1917 after his predecessor Oscar De Priest, he became the second African American to serve on the City Council and served as Mayor William Hale Thompson's floor leader throughout the 1920s. In 1922 he had his house built at 3800 South Calumet Avenue, a Flemish Revival house in what is now the landmarked Giles-Calumet District. He did not run for re-election in 1933, lost a 1936 congressional nomination bid to De Priest, and died of bronchial pneumonia at his Chicago home on May 28, 1946.

name: Leontyne Price
aliases: Mary Violet Leontine Price; Mary Violet Leontyne Price
description: Leontyne Price is an American lyric soprano, the first African American singer to achieve an international reputation in opera. Born February 10, 1927, in Laurel, Mississippi, she sang in her church choir as a girl, graduated from the College of Education and Industrial Arts in Wilberforce, Ohio, in 1948, and studied for four years at the Juilliard School in New York under Florence Page Kimball. She made her debut in April 1952 in a Broadway revival of Virgil Thomson's Four Saints in Three Acts, then sang Bess in the 1952 to 1954 production and tour of Porgy and Bess. In 1955 she became the first African American to sing an opera role on television, in NBC's Tosca. Her operatic stage debut came in San Francisco in 1957, followed by appearances in Vienna in 1959 and at La Scala in Milan in 1960. She debuted at the Metropolitan Opera in January 1961 as Leonora in Il Trovatore and became one of the Met's leading sopranos. Samuel Barber wrote Antony and Cleopatra for her, and she premiered it at the opening of the Met's new Lincoln Center house in 1966. She gave her farewell Aïda at the Met in 1985 and continued recitals until 1997.

name: Larry Clark
description: Larry Clark is an American filmmaker of the L.A. Rebellion, the Los Angeles School of Black Filmmakers — not Lawrence Donald Clark, the Tulsa-born photographer who directed Kids. Born in Ohio and raised in Cleveland, he took a bachelor's degree at Miami University, where he was president of the Black Student Union, then drove to Los Angeles to enrol at UCLA. Sources conflict on his MFA year: the UCLA Film & Television Archive lists 1977, while UCLA Newsroom lists 1981, and this packet does not blend them. His first feature, Passing Through (1977), made as his UCLA master's thesis film, follows jazz musician Eddie Warmack, released from prison, refusing the mob-controlled music business and seeking his mentor Poppa Harris; the Archive credits Clark as director, producer, writer and editor, and he co-wrote the screenplay with Ted Lange. The film won the Special Jury Prize at the Locarno International Film Festival and entered the National Film Registry in 2023. Earlier he directed As Above, So Below (1973); his second feature was Cutting Horse (2002). He later taught film at San Francisco State University.

name: Lauren Green
description: Lauren Green is Vice President of C&G Construction Supply Company, the Calumet City, Illinois construction-material supplier the company describes as 100% minority- and women-owned, established in 2009 and certified MBE/WBE at national, state, county and City of Chicago levels. Her vice presidency is documented on WVON's Class of 2026 roster; no independent source naming her was located in this pass, and other Chicago professionals of the same name were excluded as namesakes. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Leah Fulton
description: Leah Fulton is Vice President of Programs at Chicago Scholars, the foundation that selects, trains and mentors academically ambitious students from under-resourced Chicago communities through college completion and into civic leadership; announced on July 22, 2025 after a nationwide search, she oversees its college-access and college-success programming. She holds a PhD in Higher Education from the University of Minnesota, brings sixteen years in higher-education leadership, and previously served as Vice President for Student Life at Trinity Christian College in Palos Heights. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
